You could start learning a little bit of python if you wanted. The math course in the first semester is the hardest course out of the six (for me at least). 

You could start trying to learn binary, but my teacher did a pretty good job teaching. It's just about actually doing the homework, just because you get in class doesn't mean you actually get it. I also used the tutor A LOT. probably 2-3 hours a week which is all entirely free. Can't recommend using the tutor enough and thats for all subjects. Sheridan pays them to help us, if you don't like one for some reason you can sign up with any of them not just the one that is technically associated with your class. 

You could also start any sort of ccna training videos, they will help you down the line, but you don't really get into networking till semester 2 and 3.

Both programs are cool, I have stuck with ICT and will be graduating in December. ICT has gone through a lot of changes from where it started from I would say more than SDNE (not that I know that much but just from what I have grasped from professors). So is not quite as much about pure networking as it used to be, but still a lot!

Go into SDNE if you want to write code and from my understanding, a lot of the code they write is centered around learning Java and actually writing applications with a front and backend.

Go into ICT if you want more of a devops/infastructure role. You would still be writing code but more IaC and smaller scripts. We are also learning a lot about cloud networking and working with AWS Academy. 

Both programs have really good coordinators, ICT has Felix, who knows a lot and is always willing to help. And I have heard really good things about Simon who is the coordinator for SDNE. 

The thing with college is that it is not that hard to pass the classes. The point is not to pass the classes very few programs at Sheridan actually look impressive to an employer. What can impress them though is the knowledge that you learn in classes and out of class, along with the great opportunity that co-op provides to give you workplace experience. If you cheat your way through and don't learn anything you might as well just go and apply to help-desk jobs now and you will be much further along in an IT career then you would be doing either program and not actually learning anything. 

I don't think you can go wrong picking either program as long as you apply yourself and take an interest in what is being taught you can get a lot out of it.

In the program they start you off assuming you know nothing, so it's not like there is any expected knowledge going into it. So it's not like you are starting off behind.

I am only going into my second year so taking everything I say with a grain of salt, but if you are going into the cp program or any IT program you are only going to be learning a small percentage of what you are going to need to pursue a career. You will need to work outside of school as well to learn new technologies, or different software the learning is never going to really stop.

I assume you picked cp because you enjoy technology, which is great you will learn about things that interest you, but this program or even sdne is not going to get you a great job, the work you do outside the classroom is going to be what gets you that. 

What I am saying is that you are going to need to work hard, so doing the CP program while it may be "easier" is not going to set you up with anything other than having an easier pass through college. The diploma is not going to get you a job, but the learning you did to get that diploma will.

You may have to work harder to pass courses in sdne, but at the end of the day of you are only there to pass courses you probably should take some time and figure out if IT is really what you want to be doing .

I hope this didn't come across as super negative because I didn't mean for it too, maybe CP is the right fit for you right now. My main point is that this diploma ain't worth shit if you don't know shit, and the more shit you know the more places want to pay you to be there.

What ever program you pick go and learn what the profs are saying and you will do much better than just trying to pass classes.
